content: Juice is a liquid that is naturally present within the tissues of fruits or vegetables. It is typically extracted by mechanically squeezing or crushing fresh fruits or vegetables without the use of heat or chemical solvents. For instance, orange juice is the liquid derived from the fruit of the orange tree. Juice can be made at home using fresh fruits and vegetables with the help of manual or electric juicers. Many commercially available juices are filtered to remove fiber or pulp, although high-pulp fresh orange juice is also marketed as an alternative. Some juices are sold in concentrated forms, often frozen, requiring the consumer to add water to reconstitute the liquid to its original state. Concentrates generally have a distinct taste compared to their fresh-squeezed counterparts. Other juices are reconstituted before being packaged for retail sale. Common methods for preserving and processing fruit juices include canning, pasteurization, freezing, evaporation, and spray drying. Popular juices include apple, orange, grapefruit, pineapple, tomato, mango, carrot, grape, cranberry, and pomegranate. It has become increasingly common to combine multiple fruits into single juice beverages. Popular blends include combinations like cranberry-apple and apple-blackcurrant. Prepackaged single-fruit juices have lost market share to prepackaged fruit juice blends. Several companies have successfully capitalized on this trend by offering prepackaged fruit juice combinations. Examples include Innocent and P&J in the UK and Nudie in Australia. Juice bars, which offer freshly made fruit juices, have also become widespread in many Western countries. These establishments often claim that freshly made juices provide superior health benefits. This claim is based on the idea that antioxidants in the juice begin to react with oxygen free radicals immediately after juicing, thereby diminishing their health benefits over time. Juice is also widely used in cooking recipes around the world. Lime and lemon juice are particularly popular for adding a slightly sour or bitter flavor to dishes. Juice labeling often adheres to specific standards of purity, with many countries requiring that products labeled as juice contain 100% fruit juice. In the UK, the term fruit juice can only legally describe a product that is 100% fruit juice, as mandated by the Fruit Juices and Fruit Nectars Regulations of 2003. However, the term juice drink can be used for beverages that include juice, even if the juice content is as low as 1% of the total volume. In the USA, the term fruit juice is also legally restricted to products that are 100% fruit juice. In international trade, diluted juices are often labeled as beverages containing fruit juice or puree, water, and sometimes sweeteners. In New Zealand, juice typically refers to a sweetened fruit extract, while nectar denotes a pure fruit or vegetable extract. However, juice labels can be misleading, with companies often obscuring the actual content. Labels such as no added sugar are common, but these products are frequently made from reconstituted concentrates, which behave similarly to added sugars. Additionally, the naturally occurring fructose in these products can still be unhealthy for consumers. It is often difficult for consumers to determine the exact contents of juice concentrates. Juice does not typically contain carbonation, although some carbonated beverages, like Orangina, include actual fruit juice as an ingredient. Juices are often consumed for their perceived health benefits. For example, orange juice is a rich source of vitamin C, while prune juice is associated with digestive health benefits. Cranberry juice has long been recognized for its ability to prevent or treat bladder infections, as it contains a substance that inhibits bacteria from adhering to the bladder lining. Overall, fruit juice consumption has increased in Europe, Australia, New Zealand, and the USA in recent years, likely due to the public perception of juices as a healthy, natural source of nutrients and a growing interest in health-related issues. However, the belief that fruit juice is as beneficial as consuming fresh fruit has been questioned, primarily due to the lack of fiber and the processing involved. The high levels of fructose in fruit juice, when consumed without fiber, have been suggested as a contributing factor to the rising diabetes epidemic in Western countries. High-fructose corn syrup, a common ingredient in many juice cocktails, has also been linked to the increased prevalence of type II diabetes. Additionally, excessive juice consumption has been associated with weight gain.
